<reason>B opened with a vivid, well-framed case ($11 vs $14 burger, "chosen vs extracted") and skillfully narrowed "rival" to "the restaurant's own channel," neutralizing A's early slippery-slope framing. But B's most decisive weapon—the "confession" dichotomy in B4.5 (either the premium is genuine value and no volume is lost, or lost volume proves ignorance)—was cleanly escaped by A's loss-aversion/salience argument in A4.1, which showed order abandonment can occur from last-second friction regardless of whether the original price was fair. B's closing simply re-asserted the confession framing without engaging that escape, which the rules flag as a real weakness (repeating earlier points, ignoring live pressure). A also introduced an asymmetric-verification point (transaction-tested app-menu prices vs. never-tested counter prices) that B never rebutted after it appeared, and A's "marketing funds discovery" economic argument about restaurants losing acquisition support went largely unanswered throughout. B also incurred two clipped-for-length turns versus A's one, a real execution cost. On balance, A built the more resilient, adapted case by the end, even though B's rhetoric and opening framing were sharper.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's loss-aversion answer (A4.1) to B's "confession" dichotomy (B4.5) was the pivotal exchange: it defused B's cleanest trap, and B's closing failed to re-engage it, instead repeating the confession framing verbatim.</best_rebuttal>
